concept.name: Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins
concept.title: Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins

spark.summary: A Point-in-Time ML Feature Store eliminates training-serving skew and temporal data leakage by pairing a low-latency online key-value store with an immutable offline time-travel lakehouse queried via ASOF joins.
spark.keyTakeaway: When data scientists join a label table (e, never join training labels with the latest feature value; always align each observation timestamp against the most recent feature snapshot written strictly before the label event.
spark.byteSummary:
Production ML models frequently degrade in live traffic because offline training datasets accidentally include future feature values—a bug known as temporal data leakage—or compute aggregations differently from online serving paths. A Point-in-Time Feature Store solves both problems through a unified Feature Registry and dual-sink materialization.

In the offline path, historical feature mutations are appended with an event_timestamp and a created_timestamp into Apache Iceberg or Parquet tables. When generating training sets, an ASOF JOIN (as-of join) matches each label timestamp to the latest feature record where feature_timestamp <= event_timestamp within a bounded lookback TTL.

In the online path, Apache Flink computes identical sliding-window aggregations (such as 5-minute transaction velocity) and writes the latest state to Redis Cluster for sub-5ms p99 inference lookups, while asynchronously flushing immutable history to the offline lakehouse.

learningJourney.title: Training-Serving Skew & Temporal Leakage
learningJourney.purpose: Diagnose why naive SQL joins corrupt offline training datasets with future information.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Training-Serving Skew & Temporal Leakage** as the intuition layer for Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins: Diagnose why naive SQL joins corrupt offline training datasets with future information.
explanation.core: When data scientists join a label table (e.g., fraud_labels at t=12:00) against a mutable feature table (user_profiles), they read the user's current state rather than the state at t=12:00. This leaks post-event outcomes into training, inflating offline AUC while causing severe online accuracy drops.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, training-serving skew & temporal leakage becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.

learningJourney.codeExample:
SELECT l.entity_id, l.event_ts, f.tx_count_1h
FROM fraud_labels l
ASOF JOIN user_features f
  MATCH_CONDITION (l.event_ts >= f.feature_ts)
  ON l.entity_id = f.entity_id;

learningJourney.title: Unified Feature Registry & Schema Contracts
learningJourney.purpose: Define declarative feature views once to guarantee identical online and offline semantics.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Unified Feature Registry & Schema Contracts** as the intuition layer for Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins: Define declarative feature views once to guarantee identical online and offline semantics.
explanation.core: A central Feature Registry stores typed entity keys, aggregation windows, null-handling defaults, and serialization schemas (Protobuf/Avro). Both Spark batch backfills and Flink streaming jobs compile from the same transformation definition, preventing subtle SQL-vs-Python drift.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, unified feature registry & schema contracts becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When data scientists join a label table (e, never join training labels with the latest feature value; always align each observation timestamp against the most recent feature snapshot written strictly before the label event.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: Dual-Sink Streaming Materialization
learningJourney.purpose: Write real-time Flink aggregations to Redis online and Iceberg offline without divergence.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Dual-Sink Streaming Materialization** as the intuition layer for Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins: Write real-time Flink aggregations to Redis online and Iceberg offline without divergence.
explanation.core: Apache Flink ingests Kafka events, maintains keyed sliding windows in RocksDB state backends, and emits updates to a Dual-Sink Materializer. Online writes use pipelined Redis HSET/MSET with TTLs for sub-5ms lookups, while offline writes buffer into Apache Iceberg Parquet files via two-phase commit.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, dual-sink streaming materialization becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.

learningJourney.title: Low-Latency Online Feature Serving
learningJourney.purpose: Serve multi-entity feature vectors in under 5ms p99 at 100K+ QPS.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Low-Latency Online Feature Serving** as the intuition layer for Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins: Serve multi-entity feature vectors in under 5ms p99 at 100K+ QPS.
explanation.core: Inference services fetch 50–200 features per request across multiple entities (user, merchant, device). Packing features into compact binary blobs or Redis Hashes per feature-view, batching lookups via MGET/pipeline, and pinning hot keys in local L1 in-memory caches keeps p99 latency under 5ms.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, low-latency online feature serving becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.

learningJourney.title: On-Demand Request-Time Transformations
learningJourney.purpose: Compute context-dependent features at inference time without pre-materialization.

explanation.foundation: Think of **On-Demand Request-Time Transformations** as the intuition layer for Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins: Compute context-dependent features at inference time without pre-materialization.
explanation.core: Features like distance_between(user_gps, merchant_gps) or amount / user_avg_spend_30d depend on live request payloads and cannot be pre-computed. On-Demand Feature Views execute lightweight stateless Python/C++ expressions inside the serving process right after online store hydration.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, on-demand request-time transformations becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.

learningJourney.title: Online-Offline Parity & Drift Monitoring
learningJourney.purpose: Detect silent skew between Redis serving vectors and Iceberg historical snapshots.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Online-Offline Parity & Drift Monitoring** as the intuition layer for Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins: Detect silent skew between Redis serving vectors and Iceberg historical snapshots.
explanation.core: Even with shared definitions, late-arriving Kafka events or Redis evictions can cause online-offline drift. A Parity Auditor samples 1% of live inference feature logs, writes them to Iceberg, and runs a daily Wasserstein / PSI distribution diff against batch-recomputed values.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, online-offline parity & drift monitoring becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.

learningJourney.title: Backfilling & Zero-Downtime Schema Evolution
learningJourney.purpose: Hydrate months of historical state for new features without impacting live inference.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Backfilling & Zero-Downtime Schema Evolution** as the intuition layer for Point-in-Time ML Feature Store & ASOF Joins: Hydrate months of historical state for new features without impacting live inference.
explanation.core: Launching a new feature requires backfilling 6–12 months of Iceberg history via partitioned Spark jobs and seeding Redis before traffic cutover. Using shadow feature keys and atomic pointer swaps in the Feature Registry ensures live models never read partially backfilled state.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, backfilling & zero-downtime schema evolution becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.

learningJourney.codeExample:
def backfill_partition(spark, date_str, target_table):
    df = spark.read.table('raw_events').filter(f"dt = '{date_str}'")
    agg = compute_window_features(df)
    agg.write.format('iceberg').mode('overwrite').option('replaceWhere', f"dt='{date_str}'").save(target_table)

knowledgeChecks.question: A fraud model achieves 0.96 AUC in offline evaluation but drops to 0.71 AUC in production. Inspection shows training used a standard SQL LEFT JOIN on user_id against the mutable user_stats table. What caused the drop?

options.text: Temporal data leakage from joining labels with post-event feature mutations
options.feedback: Correct! Joining against a mutable table leaks future outcomes into historical training rows; an ASOF JOIN on feature_ts <= event_ts fixes this.

options.text: Redis key eviction during offline Spark training
options.feedback: Offline Spark training reads from the Iceberg/Parquet offline store, not Redis.

options.text: Insufficient L1 cache TTL in the online inference service
options.feedback: L1 cache TTL affects online latency and slight staleness, not a 0.25 AUC offline-to-online collapse.

options.text: Using Protobuf serialization instead of JSON for feature vectors
options.feedback: Serialization format affects payload size and CPU, not model AUC.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Mutable table joins leak future state into past training labels. Point-in-time ASOF joins enforce feature_ts <= event_ts.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a production Feature Store pack multiple features of the same entity view into a single Redis Hash or Protobuf blob instead of storing one Redis key per feature?

options.text: To bypass Apache Iceberg compaction limits
options.feedback: Iceberg compaction applies to the offline Parquet store, not Redis key layout.

options.text: To reduce network round-trips and memory overhead per key metadata
options.feedback: Correct! Packing a feature view into one key cuts Redis RTTs and per-key hash-table overhead by an order of magnitude.

options.text: To eliminate the need for Flink checkpointing
options.feedback: Flink checkpointing is still required for stateful stream fault tolerance.

options.text: To allow SQL ASOF joins directly inside Redis
options.feedback: Redis is an online key-value store and does not execute historical ASOF joins.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Co-locating features per entity view minimizes network round-trips and Redis per-key memory overhead.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which metric and action is best suited for detecting silent online-offline feature distribution drift in production?

options.text: Monitor Redis CPU utilization and scale up shards
options.feedback: CPU utilization measures compute load, not feature value distribution skew.

options.text: Disable Flink sliding windows and switch to daily batch
options.feedback: Switching to daily batch breaks real-time freshness requirements.

options.text: Compute Population Stability Index (PSI) between 1% logged online vectors and offline recomputations
options.feedback: Correct! Comparing logged online vectors against offline recomputations via PSI/KS detects silent skew and triggers backfills.

options.text: Increase the ASOF join lookback TTL to 365 days
options.feedback: Extending lookback TTL can actually mask missing fresh data rather than detect drift.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Logging 1% of live served vectors and comparing them to offline recomputations via PSI directly measures online-offline parity.

beginner.summary: A feature store acts like a shared pantry for ML models: it saves pre-computed stats once so both model training and live predictions use the exact same numbers.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When data scientists join a label table (e, never join training labels with the latest feature value; always align each observation timestamp against the most recent feature snapshot written strictly before the label event.
beginner.byteSummary:
Think of a Feature Store as a dual-purpose database for machine learning. Training needs months of history to learn patterns, while live apps need answers in milliseconds.

By keeping a fast Redis cache for live traffic and an Iceberg history log for training—both fed by the same pipeline—teams avoid bugs where the model sees different numbers in testing than in production.

intermediate.summary: Point-in-Time Feature Stores combine Flink streaming aggregations, Redis online serving (<5ms p99), and Iceberg ASOF joins to guarantee online-offline parity.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When data scientists join a label table (e, never join training labels with the latest feature value; always align each observation timestamp against the most recent feature snapshot written strictly before the label event.
intermediate.byteSummary:
Modern ML platforms separate feature engineering from model serving using a central Feature Registry. Flink computes sliding-window aggregates into Redis (online) and Iceberg (offline).

During training, Spark executes ASOF joins (feature_ts <= event_ts) to reconstruct leak-free historical snapshots, while online inference uses Protobuf key packing and circuit-breaker fallbacks.

advanced.summary: Enterprise feature stores enforce strict bi-temporal ASOF semantics, checkpointed 2PC dual-sink materialization, L1-cached Protobuf serving, and automated PSI parity auditing.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When data scientists join a label table (e, never join training labels with the latest feature value; always align each observation timestamp against the most recent feature snapshot written strictly before the label event.
advanced.byteSummary:
At 100K+ QPS and petabyte offline scale, dual-write consistency requires checkpointed Flink 2PC commits to Iceberg paired with bounded-retry Redis pipelines and DLQs.

On-demand request-time UDFs bridge stored state with ephemeral context, while shadow namespaces and atomic registry pointer swaps enable zero-downtime backfills.
